story_variants.en:
## Tame the Chaos!

Your Downloads folder has 200+ files — screenshots, PDFs, memes, random ZIPs. Sound familiar?

Let's write a Python script that **automatically organizes files** by their extension into neat folders.

### What You'll Learn
- Working with `os` and `shutil` modules
- File path manipulation with `pathlib`
- Dictionary mapping for file categories
- Looping through directory contents

### The Plan
1. Define file categories (images, docs, videos, etc.)
2. Scan a directory for all files
3. Create category folders if they don't exist
4. Move each file to its matching folder

> **Real-world impact:** This script can save you hours every month. Many developers use variations of this daily!

explanation.en: Import os for directory operations and shutil for moving files
Import Path for clean file path handling
Now let's define our file categories...
Create a dictionary mapping category names to file extensions
Image files go into the Images folder
Code files get their own folder too!
Dictionary complete — each key is a folder, values are extensions
Point to the Downloads folder (works on any OS)
Loop through every item in the directory
Get the file extension in lowercase (.jpg, .pdf, etc.)
Check each category to find where this file belongs
Match found! This file belongs in this category
Create the folder if it doesn't exist yet
Move the file into its category folder!

executionSteps.description: Map folder names to file extensions
Loop through all items in Downloads folder
Check if item is a file (skip directories)
Create Images/ folder if it doesn't exist
Move file to its category folder

instruction.en: Write a script that prints the extension of each file in a list. Use a for loop and string slicing or the .split() method.

hints.en: You can get the extension with file.split('.')[-1] or file[file.rfind('.'):]

quiz.q: Which module is used to move files in Python?
What does exist_ok=True do in mkdir()?

under_the_hood.summary: The organizer lists directory entries, maps each file's extension to a category folder, and moves it; on the same disk a move only rewrites a directory entry, so no file data is copied.

steps.title: Listing reads directory entries
steps.body: A folder on disk is itself a small table of entries: a name plus a pointer to the file's data (an inode on Linux and macOS). Path('Downloads').iterdir() asks the OS for those entries and yields one Path per name. It does not open or read the files themselves, so listing 200 files is fast.

steps.title: Extension -> category is a dict lookup
steps.body: For 'Holiday.JPG', path.suffix is '.JPG'; lowering it gives '.jpg'. A dict built once, such as {'.jpg': 'Images', '.png': 'Images', '.pdf': 'Documents'}, maps it to 'Images' in one O(1) lookup. Unknown suffixes fall through to a default like 'Others' with .get(ext, 'Others').

props.title: Built once, looked up for every file

steps.title: mkdir(exist_ok=True) makes it safe to re-run
steps.body: Before moving, the script creates the target folder. exist_ok=True means 'do nothing if it is already there' instead of raising FileExistsError, so running the organizer twice is harmless. parents=True also creates any missing parent folders.

steps.title: A move on the same disk is a rename
steps.body: shutil.move first tries os.rename. When source and target are on the same filesystem, rename just removes the name from the Downloads entry table and adds it to the Images table; the file's bytes never move, so even a 4 GB video moves instantly. Across drives, rename fails and shutil.move falls back to copying the data and then deleting the original.

left.label: Same filesystem
left.code:
os.rename:
- add entry 'Images/Holiday.jpg'
- remove entry 'Holiday.jpg'
file data untouched

right.label: Different filesystem
right.code:
copy every byte to the new disk
then delete the original
(slow for big files)

steps.title: Watch out for name clashes
steps.body: If Images/report.pdf already exists, the behaviour depends on the OS: on Linux and macOS a rename silently replaces the existing file, while on Windows it raises an error. A careful organizer checks target.exists() first and adds a suffix such as report (1).pdf.

under_the_hood.takeaway: Organizing files is mostly moving names between directory tables. Know that a same-disk move is a cheap rename and that it can overwrite silently, and your script will be both fast and safe.
